ACT-EN2C-P1-Q01.note: Conventions. The comma is the best mark, but the colon is defensible and I can write the defense, so this drops. The explanation's rebuttal of "pattern:" is simply wrong: it says the colon "would need an independent clause in front of it, and 'whose bench turns out no parts' is a relative clause that cannot stand alone." The test is not whether the relative clause stands alone, it is whether ALL the text before the colon forms a sentence. "The second bay past the scale house belongs to Odile Bracht, whose bench turns out no parts, only a pattern" is a complete sentence (subject "The second bay past the scale house," verb "belongs"), and a colon after a complete clause introducing an amplifying appositive is standard edited usage (CMOS 6.61, 6.63) and is a shape the ACT itself keys. The trailing ", pressed into damp sand..." sits comfortably inside the post-colon element. Two defensible marks. FOUR-WORDS-AFTER: partial shortcut. The next four words are "a wooden double of" - a bare noun phrase, which kills "pattern;" outright (nothing independent follows) and kills the unpunctuated option by ear, leaving comma vs colon from the post-blank window alone. 4 options -> 2 without reading the passage.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q02.note: Conventions, subject-verb agreement. "Half the patterns" is a fraction subject that takes its number from the noun it quantifies, so plural; "on her rack" is the intervening trap. "are" is the only plural form offered, so no second option survives - "was" fails on number as well as tense, "is"/"has been" on number. Medium rather than easy because it stacks the fraction-subject rule on the intervening-prepositional-phrase rule. FOUR-WORDS-AFTER: clean. The next four words are "older than the furnace" - a predicate adjective that carries no number information. The resolving noun ("patterns") is BEFORE the blank, so the item cannot be solved from the post-blank window.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q03.note: Knowledge of Language, word precision. "gradually" is right and no second option is defensible: "suddenly" and "quickly" are flatly contradicted by the eleven hours and "intermittently" by "the whole time." But exclusivity is not the problem here - discrimination is. FOUR-WORDS-AFTER: FULL SHORTCUT, the recorded defect in its strongest form. The next four words are "over the eleven hours," which decide the item on their own: a duration of eleven hours rules out suddenly, quickly and intermittently without the solver reading any other part of the sentence, the paragraph or the passage. All three distractors die in the same four-word window, which is why I score the distractors weak and the difficulty easy against a real 50/35 section. This is the item I would rewrite first on the Conventions/KoL side - either move the duration evidence out of the adjacent clause, or offer distractors that the duration does not settle (e.g. "steadily" vs "unevenly" would at least force "the whole time" to be read).

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q04.pick: Yes, because it opens the distinction that paragraph 3 builds its whole account on.
ACT-EN2C-P1-Q04.note: Production of Writing, adding material. With the source in hand the key is uniquely right: paragraph 2 ends on one undifferentiated oversize allowance, paragraph 3 immediately splits it by metal and gives Bracht a rule per metal, so the added sentence is the hinge. A is refuted by the sentence itself (it names no number), C is refuted because paragraph 2 never fixes a fraction, D by paragraphs 4 and 5 where the metals return as stamped numbers and as the silicon bronze. So it survives a with-source grade. ON THE AUTHOR'S FLAG: I agree, and I think it is worse than the free 50% they describe. The 2-Yes/2-No frame controls direction but not the leak, because the options still differ along the axis the stem names - four different rhetorical acts (supplies a datum / links to the next paragraph / protects an established focus / denies relevance), one per option, so the act the stem asks for is identifiable without the passage. Three specific blind routes: (i) the stem QUOTES the sentence, so a blind solver reads "The fraction is not the same for every metal," sees no number in it, and kills A from the stem alone - that is one option gone with zero passage access; (ii) D is an absolute denial ("not a subject this essay returns to"), the distractor family blind solvers discard on sight; (iii) C asserts a specific prior state ("has settled on one fixed fraction") which is the over-specific shape solvers reject, and it directly contradicts A, so a solver who prefers the survivor of a contradicted pair lands on the Yes side anyway. What remains, B, is also the generic forward-link rationale that is correct on most add-a-sentence items. I would expect this to sit at or above the 76% stratum figure, not at 50%. SEPARATE DEFECT, with-source: the added sentence opens "The fraction" with a definite article for a fraction paragraph 2 has never introduced (paragraph 2 says only "a hair too small"). The sentence the writer is asked to judge is itself cohesively broken; that does not change the key, but it is not ACT-grade prose and it makes A's premise ("has so far withheld") the only true premise among the wrong options, which is an awkward place for truth to sit.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q05.note: Conventions, sentence boundaries. Two independent clauses with no conjunction: the semicolon is the only mark that joins them. The colon is not a live second answer - the pre-colon text is independent, but the second clause sets a different metal beside the first rather than amplifying or itemizing it, which is what a colon promises. Comma splice and fusion both fail. Exclusive. FOUR-WORDS-AFTER: strong partial shortcut. The next four words are "aluminum shrinks nearly twice" - a fresh subject plus a finite verb, which tells a solver an independent clause follows and kills both "shrinks," and bare "shrinks" immediately; only the colon needs a further beat of reading. 4 -> 2 from the post-blank window, and standard test-taking habit closes the rest. PASSAGE NOTE (not an exclusivity problem): "Bronze shrinks" with no quantity, sitting between gray iron's eighth of an inch per foot and aluminum's "nearly twice as much as gray iron," is thin - it reads like a clause that lost its measure. Worth a pass by the author.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q06.note: Conventions, parallel structure. "would mean" governs "doing ... , checking ... , and ___", so the third item must be a gerund. No second option survives: "weighed" and "weighs" are finite forms with no available subject, and "to weigh" breaks the series. Medium rather than hard - the series is long, but two of the three distractors are eliminable on form alone without locating the governing verb, so the item is really a 2-way between "to weigh" and "weighing." FOUR-WORDS-AFTER: clean. The next four words are "a scrapped pour against," an object phrase that fits all four options equally; the evidence ("doing," "checking") is entirely upstream of the blank, which is how this family should be built.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q07.note: Production of Writing, transitions. The relation is substitution - no manual, and in its place a strip of tape - so "Instead." I considered defending "No Change" and rejected it: concessive "Still" needs the second sentence to push back against the first, and "the only list ... is a strip of tape" continues in the same direction (the scheme is undocumented) rather than countering it. "Therefore" makes the missing manual cause the tape; "In addition" adds the tape to a manual the previous sentence denies. Exclusive. Easy: the previous sentence is an explicit negation, which is the clearest possible cue for a substitution connector. Not a Conventions/KoL item, but for the record the post-blank window ("the only list of") does not resolve it - the cue is the preceding sentence.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q08.note: Conventions, possessives. One shop throughout the essay, so the singular possessive. "shops" marks no possession, "shops'" invents multiple shops, bare "shop" leaves an attributive noun with no ownership mark. Exclusive - nothing in the passage supports a plural reading. FOUR-WORDS-AFTER: partial shortcut. Only one word follows before the period - "door" - and it is enough to establish that a possessive is wanted, killing "shops" and "shop" from the post-blank window. It does NOT choose between "shop's" and "shops'"; that needs the passage's single foundry. 4 -> 2, which is the acceptable end of this defect.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q09.note: Knowledge of Language, word precision, and the best-built item in the batch. The two following sentences supply a basis (the published figure for the nearest metal) and a subsequent correction (the casting measured cold), which is exactly an estimate; "guess" and "hunch" deny any basis. CLOSEST CALL IN THE BATCH: I nearly spent a false on "assumption" - she applies another metal's figure to an alloy on the unverified premise that they behave alike, and she then tests that premise, so the explanation's rebuttal ("taken for granted rather than something the shop deliberately sets out to test") is backwards, since testing is what one does to assumptions. What saved it is the syntactic frame rather than the semantics: "sized from a ___" takes a quantity, and "guess" and "estimate" are quantities while "hunch" and "assumption" are propositions. The frame filters to two and precision picks one. I score it exclusive, but the author should know the key rests on the frame, not on the explanation as written - if that sentence is ever reworded away from "sized from," the item goes to two answers. FOUR-WORDS-AFTER: clean, and the reason the item is hard. The blank ends its sentence, so there is no post-blank window at all; resolution requires the next TWO sentences. This is the pattern the other KoL item (Q03) should be rebuilt toward.

ACT-EN2C-P1-Q10.note: Production of Writing, sentence placement. [A] is the better answer - the added sentence is a general premise and belongs in front of the instance - but [B] is defensible and this drops. The defense: at [B] the sentence sits between the problem and the workaround, explaining the just-asserted "sized from a guess" and then handing off to "Bracht takes the published figure for the nearest metal she pours." That is premise-after-consequence order, entirely ordinary in edited prose, and it creates a tight adjacent lexical link on "published figure" that [A] does not have (at [A] the phrase is two sentences downstream). The explanation's rebuttal - "dropped after it, the sentence explains a problem the paragraph has already begun solving" - is not true of [B]: at [B] nothing has yet been solved, the only thing stated is that the sizing is a guess, and explaining WHY it is a guess is precisely what the sentence does there. [C] and [D] are correctly dead ([C] cuts the two-step cut-and-wait / measure-cold procedure in half, [D] arrives after the premise has been used up), so this is a genuine 2-way, not a 4-way. Fixing it means making [B] hostile - e.g. give sentence [B] an explicit backward connector so that inserting anything between it and the opener breaks the reference.
